newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street should pay for illegal profits - localities.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street should pay for illegal profits - localities.

text.p: The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority on Tuesday urged U.S. regulators to force Wall Street firms to pay back up to $1 billion in allegedly illegal profits they earned from complex bond deals since 1990.
The Internal Revenue Service is going after state and local governments for taxes they did not realise they had to pay when the bond refinancing deals were arranged.
Municipalities say they are not liable since they were deceived by bond underwriters, who made big profits in the process.

Municipalities were "exploited and deceived" by Wall Street banks that "profited handsomely" in the process, lawyers for the authority said. Localities nationwide face "dire consequences" if forced to pay, it said.

Municipalities are generally not allowed to invest proceeds from tax-exempt bond issues in taxable U.S. Treasury securities with higher yields. An exception is when profits from the Treasury bonds are used to pay off outstanding municipal bonds with higher rates. Any excess profits from such a refinancing must be turned over to the IRS.
As interest rates dropped in the early 1990s, thousands of municipalities cut their debt service costs by selling new bonds at lower rates and buying Treasury securities to pay off their old bonds.

But many states and localities were not aware they had excess profits because Wall Street firms that arranged the refinancings overcharged them for the Treasury securities, the authority said in a 43-page letter to the IRS.

In the past year, probes of specific refinancings turned up alleged overcharges by Wall Street firms. The probes were triggered in the wake of charges by whisteblower Michael Lissack, a former Wall Street investment banker.
Los Angeles County did one such investigation and filed a lawsuit, along with Lissack, against the firm involved.
The Los Angeles authority said in Tuesday's letter that municipalities should not be hit with the bills since they did not know about the inflated prices.

The Michel/Shaked group, a Boston economic consulting firm that the authority hired to price 104 bond refunding deals between 1990 and 1995, found "unjustified markups" of about $4 per $1,000 bond on average.
Wall Street's top senior managers of such refundings alone made an estimated $186 million in total profits from the deals, said the economists, who did not name the firms.

But Securities Data Co., an industry data firm, said the top two underwriters were Goldman, Sachs & Co. and Merrill Lynch & Co. Inc. Officials at both brokerages were not immediately available for comment.
"This is a bombshell," the Phillips & Cohen partner John Phillips said in a telephone interview.
"There is no justification for the kind of markups the industry routinely charged," Phillips said, adding that the $1 billion overcharge estimate was probably conservative.

Last April, the Los Angeles County authority filed a $14 million lawsuit against Lazard Freres & Co. in the first court challenge to the alleged Wall Street overcharges, dubbed "yield burning" by municipal bond market participants.
The economists said no U.S. state or territory was spared from yield burning damages.

According to a a state-by-state breakdown in the study, California tops the damages list, with $88.8 million; followed by New York, with $82.1 million; Texas, $70.3 million; and Florida, $58.5 million.
South Dakota, the Virgin Islands, North Dakota, Montana and Wyoming have the smallest bills, the study says.

The Los Angeles authority said municipalities are not the only victims of yield burning. "Yield burning has clearly damaged the U.S. Treasury" because the inflated prices artifically depressed the yields on Treasury securities used in refinancings, the comment letter says.
"The money the federal government lost to yield burning went -- dollar for dollar -- directly into the pockets of the nation's wealthiest Wall Sstreet investment banking firms," the authority said.
